0.note: See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The term that the ULT translates as **Weakness** could be the name of the tune of this psalm. It might also be a musical instruction indicating that singers should perform the song in a minor key or in a somber tone. Alternate translation: [perform in a minor key] or [perform in a somber tone]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

1.note: The psalmist is not referring to a specific **fool**. He means foolish people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [A foolish person]
Here the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [thinks]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [There is no God]
The pronoun **They** refers to foolish people who deny God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Such foolish people are corrupt]

The psalmist is using the adjective **good** as a noun to mean a certain kind of action. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase, here and in verse 3. Alternate translation: [good things]

2.note: The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]
Since the psalmist has already used the name “God” earlier in this sentence, it may be more natural in your language to use a pronoun here. Alternate translation: [one seeking him]

3.note: The pronoun **him** refers back to “man” in the previous verse. It may be helpful to use a term in your translation that will clarify this for your readers. Another possibility would be to use a plural pronoun, as the psalmist does in the next sentence. Alternate translation: [All of mankind has turned away] or [All of them have turned away]

The psalmist is speaking as if people had physically **turned away** from God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [All of them have abandoned God]

The psalmist is saying **none** and **not even one** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [All people are sinful]

4.q: הֲ⁠לֹ֥א יָדְעוּ֮ פֹּ֤עֲלֵ֫י אָ֥וֶן אֹכְלֵ֣י עַ֭מִּ⁠י אָ֣כְלוּ לֶ֑חֶם
4.note: The psalmist is using the question form to express amazement that wicked people oppress others without recognizing that God will judge and punish them for doing that. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [They ought to know better, the doers of iniquity, the ones eating my people as they eat bread!]

The point of this comparison is that just as someone can **eat bread** easily and quickly, so these **doers of iniquity** readily oppress and exploit vulnerable people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the ones eating my people as readily as they eat bread]

The psalmist is speaking as if these **doers of iniquity** were actually **eating** the **people** of his nation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones exploiting my people as readily as they eat bread]

5.note: The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [they feared greatly]

5.q: אֱלֹהִ֗ים פִּ֭זַּר עַצְמ֣וֹת חֹנָ֑⁠ךְ הֱ֝בִשֹׁ֗תָה כִּֽי־אֱלֹהִ֥ים מְאָסָֽ⁠ם
5.note: The psalmist is addressing the nation of Israel as if it were an individual, even though he knows that it cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to anyone who hears this song that he feels very strongly about how God defeated and destroyed this attacking army. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if the psalmist were speaking objectively about this army. Alternate translation: [God scattered the bones of the ones encamping against Israel. The Israelites have shamed them, for God despises them]

The psalmist is using the fact that the surviving soldiers of this army were not able to bury their fellow soldiers who were killed, so that their **bones** were left **scattered** on the field of battle, to represent how completely God defeated this army. Alternate translation: [God completely defeated and destroyed]

The psalmist is using one person who was involved in **encamping** against the Israelites, probably the king who commanded this army, to mean everyone who was involved. (This is clear from the way the psalmist says **them** later in this verse.) If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones encamping against you] or [the soldiers who attacked you]
The word “you” is singular in both instances in this verse, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
The pronoun **you** seems to refer in context to “Israel” in the next verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [against you, Israel. You have shamed them]

6.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Who will give that the salvation of Israel will come from Zion?]

The psalmist is using **Who will give** as a common expression of his culture to introduce a fervent wish. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [O that salvation for Israel would come from Zion!] or [I fervently wish that salvation for Israel would come from Zion!]

The psalmist is using Mount **Zion**, the location of God’s sanctuary, to represent God himself in the act of providing **salvation** for **Israel**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [O that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to provide for the salvation of Israel!] or [I fervently wish that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to provide for the salvation of Israel!]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [O that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to save Israel!] or [I fervently wish that God would act from his sanctuary on Mount Zion to save Israel!]

The word that the ULT translates as **prosperity** can also mean “captivity.” If that is the meaning, then this verse could have been added to the psalm later, after the Israelites were conquered and taken into captivity. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to follow the translation that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [When God restores the captivity of his people] or [When God brings his people back from captivity]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms. Alternate translation: [Israel will rejoice greatly] or [Jacob will be glad; indeed, Israel will rejoice]

The psalmist is using the two names of the ancestor of the Israelites, **Jacob** and **Israel**, to represent the Israelites themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The descendants of Jacob will be glad; indeed, the Israelites will rejoice]
